title: Hamish's Hidden Peanut
markdown:
At Oak Tree Primary, books rustled and lessons hummed, and the most important job in the classroom belonged to Bartholomew Buttercup, Class Pets Monitor. Bartholomew loved things neat. His feeding chart was so tidy the ants on the windowsill could have marched by it. Every creature, from the wiggly tadpole to the slow snail, had a time and a scoop, and Bartholomew marked each with a neat check.

In a cedar-smelling cage lived Hamish the hamster. His fur was a mix of brown and cream, extra fluffy, as if he were privately pleased. While other hamsters scurried and nibbled, Hamish had a sparkle that suggested he could count sunflower seeds without looking. Lately a little puzzle had begun to sit in the classroom like a crumb no one could sweep.

“And now,” Bartholomew would announce, glasses glinting, “it is time to feed Hamish. A very important moment in our busy day.” He consulted the chart, a colourful drawing of times and food. “Yes. One scoop of hamster food, just like it says. Not a bit more. Not a bit less.”

He set the shiny dish down. Hamish twitched his whiskers and looked at it as if it were a riddle. Bartholomew turned to write. When he looked back, the dish was empty, as if a tiny storm had passed through.

“Very quick,” Bartholomew would whisper, making his check, and frowning just a little, surprised. Hamish washed his paws as if he had not done a thing. There was extra puff in his fur, and a happy squeak that did not quite match one scoop of ordinary food. Bartholomew could see the puff. He could not see the reason.

Poppy the squirrel watched from a bookshelf, tail wiggling whenever a question arrived. Jun the mole watched from a spot by the wall, where a small tunnel ran under the cage. They watched Hamish. They watched the chart. They watched the food vanish.

“It is so strange, Poppy,” Jun whispered one afternoon, nose wiggling. “The chart says two o’clock. By two-oh-one it is gone. Is he a food magician?”

Poppy’s claws made tiny sounds on the shelf. “It is like he eats it before it is even there. Maybe he has a secret pocket in his cheeks.”

Their curiosity rolled downhill like an acorn. They went to Uncle Theo, a wise old badger who lived under the oak at the edge of the school garden. His home smelled of warm earth and chamomile.

“Uncle Theo,” said Poppy, hopping from foot to foot, “we have a food puzzle. Hamish’s food disappears.”

Jun nodded, gently moving a worm aside. “Bartholomew’s chart is perfect. Hamish eats faster than a raindrop in the sun.”

Uncle Theo polished his glasses with a soft cloth. He had seen many hamsters and many busy classrooms. Steam from the chamomile curled between them. “Ah. Hamish. A hamster with special tastes, perhaps. A hamster who knows what he likes.” He let the quiet hang, kind and unhurried. “Things that look organised can be worked around by a creature with a clear goal, quick paws, and a clever mind. What if he is not only eating fast? What if he is trying to keep something safe?”

Poppy’s tail buzzed. Jun’s nose stopped wiggling, which for a mole was almost a shout.

The next day, as the clock neared two, Poppy and Jun hid behind a big leafy plant near the cage. They watched closely. Bartholomew, as always, prepared the scoop with his usual care, measuring as if the chart could hear him. When the dish was set down, Hamish did not gobble. He sat up on his back legs. His nose twitched. He looked from the dish to the space just beyond it. Bartholomew, thinking the meal had begun, turned to his chart.

Hamish nudged the dish with his nose, pushing it a little further under the bedding. Then, with a hop, he turned to the other dish: a smaller one meant for the finches, sitting on the edge of his home, full of tiny colourful seeds. Hidden among them, almost invisible, was a single perfectly roasted peanut. It must have fallen from someone’s lunchbox.

Poppy gasped. Jun’s eyes went wide. Hamish, having found the prize he had been waiting for, went back to his own dish and ate his hamster food with delight. The happy look, they understood now, was not about speed. It was about getting his favourite first, before anyone noticed, before it mixed with the ordinary scoop. He had used the clock and the busy classroom. He had made room.

Bartholomew saw the dish tucked too far into the shavings. He noticed there were no peanut crumbs where Hamish usually ate. He blinked behind his glasses. A slow smile arrived, and a chuckle that was not often heard during rota time.

“Well, Hamish,” he said, shaking his head. “You are a very clever hamster with excellent taste. You certainly kept us wondering.”

Uncle Theo, peeking from near his burrow, saw the peanut, and the triumph of a well-hidden wish. He did not come in. He only nodded, as if a classroom were a place that could keep a small secret and still be tidy.

Bartholomew showed Hamish, with kind chirps and a nod, that the hamster food was perfectly good, and that the finches’ seeds were for the finches. Hamish listened, cheeks still faintly peanut-shaped. Then, with a twinkle, Bartholomew made a tiny change to the chart: a small space, almost invisible, labelled special treat. Understanding, in his neat way, a unique and slightly sneaky wish.

Poppy and Jun went back to their lessons, minds full of wonder of the quiet sort. The classroom smelled of cedar and pencil shavings. Sunlight moved across the chart. Beside Hamish’s two-o’clock check, a little extra box waited, empty for now, ready for a peanut if one should happen to fall.
characters: Hamish (a brown-and-cream classroom hamster), Poppy (a question-tailed squirrel), Jun (a floorboard mole)
